messages.content: I'm fuzzy on f-string format specs. I know {price:.2f} rounds, but how do the alignment characters, fill characters, and the sign flag actually compose? Show me the same values formatted several ways so I can see each piece.

arguments.code:
label = "apples"
qty = 7
price = 0.65
print(f"{label:>10}|{qty:<5}|{price:.2f}")
print(f"{label:<10}|{qty:>5}|{price:05.2f}")
print(f"{label:^10}|{qty:^5}|{price:+.2f}")
print(f"{'sale':-^10}")
print(f"{-42:05d} and {42:05d}")

messages.content:
Read every spec left to right as: fill, alignment, sign, width, precision, type. In the first line, ">10" right-aligns the label in a field 10 wide, "<5" left-aligns the quantity in 5, and ".2f" fixes the price at two decimals. The second line swaps the alignments and uses "05.2f": the leading 0 is not a literal zero in front, it switches on zero-padding to the width, so 0.65 renders as 00.65.

The third line shows "^" for centering and "+.2f", where "+" forces a sign on positive numbers too. "sale" with "-^10" names the fill character explicitly: a dash is the fill, "^" the alignment. The last line is the subtle one: zero-padding is sign-aware. -42 padded to width 5 becomes -0042, not 000-42 — the zeros go after the sign, because the 0 flag really means fill "0" with "=" alignment, and "=" keeps the sign at the edge. Once you see the spec as a small grammar instead of a magic string, you can compose exactly the column you want.
What are the parts of an f-string replacement field, and in what order do they go? I keep putting things in the wrong slot.

A replacement field has up to four parts, always in this order: the expression, an optional conversion, and an optional format spec introduced by a colon — f"{expression!conversion:spec}".

The expression is any Python expression: a variable, an index, a method call, arithmetic. The conversion is one of !s, !r, or !a and forces str(), repr(), or ascii() on the value before formatting; if you omit it, the value's own __format__ receives the spec directly. The format spec after the colon is interpreted by the value's type: for numbers it controls width, precision, grouping, and sign; for strings mostly width and alignment; for dates it is a strftime pattern.

Two ordering mistakes account for most confusion. First, the conversion comes before the colon, never after: f"{name!r:>10}" is right, f"{name:>10!r}" is a syntax error. Second, the spec is not universal — ".2f" means something to a float and raises on a plain string, because the spec is handed to the value's __format__, not interpreted by the f-string itself. Remember "value first, conversion second, instructions for that value's type last," and the slots stop moving around.
How do I get thousands separators in f-strings? I need both 1,234,567 style for people and a grouped form I can scan in logs, plus percentages.

The "," in a spec asks for comma grouping every three digits: 1234567 becomes 1,234,567 with no locale lookup and no string surgery. The "_" variant groups the same way with underscores, 1_234_567, which mirrors how Python lets you write numeric literals — handy in logs and debug output because the rendered text is still close to a valid literal.

Grouping composes with the rest of the spec: ",.2f" groups and fixes two decimals (1,234,567.89), and ",.0f" groups and rounds to whole units (1,234,568). The "#" flag asks for the base prefix on integer bases, so 255 renders as 0xff, 0b11111111, and 0o377 — without "#" you get the bare digits. Finally, "%" is a type of its own: it multiplies by 100 and appends the percent sign, so 0.075 at one decimal is 7.5%. One caution: the "," grouping is a fixed convention baked into the format spec, not your operating system's locale — that predictability is exactly why it is safe for output other code or other people will parse.
What do the !s, !r, and !a conversions actually change? I want to see them on the same values, including something with a newline and a non-ASCII character.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
(1, 2)
Point(x=1, y=2)
'café\nmenu'
'caf\xe9\nmenu'

The conversion decides which dunder produces the text before any format spec applies. !s calls str(): for the Point that is the friendly "(1, 2)". !r calls repr(): "Point(x=1, y=2)" — the form meant for developers, ideally unambiguous enough to reconstruct the object. On the string, !r shows the quotes and renders the newline as the two characters \n, so the value stays on one line and its exact content is visible.

!a goes one step further: ascii() is repr() with every non-ASCII character escaped, so "café" becomes 'caf\xe9\nmenu'. That is the conversion you want in logs and protocols that must survive 7-bit channels — the output is pure ASCII no matter what the data holds. Rule of thumb: default (str) for people reading results, !r for anything you might debug later, !a when the text must travel through systems that mangle Unicode. Note that a spec after the conversion applies to the converted string, so f"{p!r:>20}" pads the repr, not the object.

Older Python wouldn't let me reuse the same quote character inside an f-string expression, so I've been writing f"{d['key']}" with mixed quotes for years. Has that changed, and should I change my habit?

It changed in Python 3.12. Before that, an f-string was tokenized before it was parsed, and the string ended at the first matching quote — so inside f"..." you could not use a double quote at all, which is why f"{d["key"]}" was a syntax error and everyone learned the mixed-quote habit, plus workarounds like assigning to a variable first or using backslash escapes in the expression (which were also banned pre-3.12).

Python 3.12 (PEP 701) gave f-strings a real grammar: you may now reuse the same quote inside the expression, nest f-strings, use backslashes, and even put comments inside multi-line replacement fields. On 3.12 or later, f"{d["key"]}" is valid and reads better than the mixed-quote version.

Should you change the habit? Only where every interpreter that runs the code is 3.12+. The restriction is at parse time, so a file using the new syntax fails to even import on 3.11 — there is no graceful fallback. Libraries supporting older Pythons keep the old habit; code that is 3.12-only can relax. The mixed-quote style is never wrong, merely a little noisier, so the safe default is: match the oldest Python your project still runs.
I saw someone write f"{total=}" and it printed the expression text too. How does that self-documenting form work, and can it take a format spec?

arguments.code:
value = 42
items = [10, 20, 12]
total = sum(items)
print(f"{value=}")
print(f"{total=}")
print(f"{total / len(items)=:.2f}")
print(f"{total = }")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
value=42
total=42
total / len(items)=14.00
total = 42

Putting "=" immediately after the expression makes the f-string print the expression's source text, then "=", then the value — built for debugging, so you never again print a bare number and wonder which variable it was. f"{value=}" gives "value=42" and f"{total=}" gives "total=42". The expression can be anything, including a call or arithmetic: the third line prints the whole text "total / len(items)=14.00", with the "=.2f" showing that a format spec still applies to the value part exactly as usual.

The last line shows the one cosmetic trap: whitespace you write around the "=" is preserved verbatim, so f"{total = }" prints "total = 42". In the tight form there is no space; if you want "total = 42" you must write the spaces yourself. One more default worth knowing: without an explicit conversion, the debug form uses repr() for the value, which is why strings come out quoted — f"{name=}" prints name='ana', not name=ana. For quick instrumentation it beats print("total:", total) on both typing and clarity, and it is meant to be deleted once the bug is found, not shipped as your logging.
Can the width and precision inside a format spec come from variables? I have a report where the column width is computed at runtime.

arguments.code:
x = 1234.5678
w, p = 10, 2
print(f"{x:{w}.{p}f}")
print(f"{x:{w},.{p}f}")
name = "kiwi"
print(f"{name:*^{w}}")

messages.content:
Yes — a format spec is itself a string that gets expanded first, so any {...} inside the spec is evaluated and substituted before the outer value is formatted. f"{x:{w}.{p}f}" with w=10 and p=2 becomes the spec "10.2f", and the number prints right-aligned in width 10 as "   1234.57". The second line shows specs compose with grouping too: "{w},.{p}f" becomes "10,.2f", giving "  1,234.57".

The third line is the one people don't expect: the nested fields can supply the fill and alignment as well — "*^{w}" centers "kiwi" in width 10 padded with asterisks. This nesting goes exactly one level deep, which is enough for the real use cases: report generators that compute a column width from the widest value, precision chosen by magnitude, alignment stored in configuration. It is also the mechanism str.format uses, so the same trick works in templates: "{:{w}}".format(value, w=width). When the width logic matters, compute it once, name it well, and let the spec stay readable.
When are f-strings the wrong tool for building text? I use them for everything, including message templates we keep in a config file.

F-strings are evaluated where they are written, with the names in scope at that moment. That is exactly wrong for three common jobs.

First, templates that live outside the code — in a config file, a database, or a translations catalog. An f-string cannot be stored as data and rendered later with values that arrive at runtime; that is what str.format, format_map, and string.Template are for. Your config-file messages belong there: the template is data, the values are supplied when the message is actually sent, and translators or operators can edit the wording without a code deploy.

Second, deferred rendering. Logging is the classic case: logger.debug("value: %s", x) lets the logging framework skip formatting entirely when the level is disabled, while an f-string pays the formatting cost on every call, and worse, raises if formatting fails even when nobody would have read the message.

Third, reuse across contexts. A message rendered in five places with slightly different data wants to be a function or a template, not five f-strings that drift apart. The rule is simple: f-strings for text that is born and dies in the same few lines of code; a template mechanism the moment the wording is data, is rendered later, or is rendered somewhere else.

We store message templates as plain strings and render them with format_map. Before rendering, I need to know which fields a template actually requires, so I can validate the context. Can I inspect a template's fields without rendering it?

arguments.code:
from string import Formatter
tmpl = "Hello {name}, you have {count} new messages."
fields = [field for _, field, _, _ in Formatter().parse(tmpl) if field]
print(fields)
ctx = {"name": "Ana", "count": 3}
print(tmpl.format_map(ctx))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
['name', 'count']
Hello Ana, you have 3 new messages.

string.Formatter().parse() is the inspector: it yields the template as a sequence of (literal_text, field_name, format_spec, conversion) tuples, and the field names are exactly what the template will demand at render time. Filtering out the None entries (the pure literal chunks) leaves ['name', 'count'] — the contract your context must satisfy. Run it when templates are loaded, not when they are sent, and a missing key becomes a startup error instead of a failed message.

Two details matter in practice. A field written as {user.name} or {items[0]} reports the full path "user.name" / "items[0]", but the context only needs the first component — split on "." and "[" when you validate. And an auto-numbered "{}" reports an empty field name, which is a sign the template should be rewritten with named fields before it goes into storage. Once the field list is known, format_map renders from any mapping — here a plain dict producing the finished sentence. Introspecting the template turns an implicit contract into a checked one.

I need a small roster printed with names centered in a banner column, IDs zero-padded, and scores that always show a sign. I can get each effect alone but the specs keep fighting each other. How do I think through combining them?

Compose the spec per column, not per line, and write each spec in the fixed order: fill+alignment, sign, zero-pad/width, precision, type. The three effects you want live in different slots, so they never actually fight — they only look tangled when written from memory.

For the centered banner name, the slot is fill and alignment: f"{name:*^12}" centers in width 12 with asterisks as fill; use "^12" alone if you want spaces. For the zero-padded ID, the slot is the 0 flag plus width: f"{id:05d}" renders 42 as 00042 — remember this is fill "0" with "=" alignment, so a negative would keep its sign at the edge. For the always-signed score, the slot is the sign flag: f"{score:+.1f}" renders +2.5 and -2.5 alike with an explicit sign.

Build a line by joining the per-column results: f"{name:*^12} {id:05d} {score:+.1f}". If a spec still surprises you, isolate it: format one value with only that spec and print repr() of the result so padding is visible. Ninety percent of "the specs are fighting" turns out to be one slot silently doing double duty — usually a stray character being read as a fill because it sits immediately before an alignment character.
We store money as integer cents everywhere. Write the display function: cents in, a string like $1,234.56 out, with correct handling of negatives and tiny amounts — no float detour.

The whole trick is to never let the value become a float. divmod on the absolute value splits cents into whole dollars and a remainder: 123456 becomes (1234, 56). The dollars get comma grouping from the "," spec, and the remainder is zero-padded to exactly two digits with "02d" — that padding is what makes 5 cents render as $0.05 instead of $0.5, and 50 as $0.50.

The sign is handled separately, from the original value, before the split: taking abs() first means divmod never sees a negative (divmod on negatives floors, which would hand you surprising remainders), and the minus sign is reattached in front of the dollar sign, where readers expect it: -$2.50, not $-2.50. Note -7 renders as -$0.07 — seven cents owed, shown exactly. Because every input is an integer and every operation is integer arithmetic, the output is exact for arbitrarily large amounts; a float version would start lying around 2**53 cents. Format from the integer at the boundary, and the display can never disagree with the stored value.
A teammate formats prices with f"${price:.2f}" where price is a float like 19.99. It looks fine. Why does our codebase insist on integer cents or Decimal for anything money-shaped?

It looks fine until it doesn't, and the failures are silent. A float cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly: 19.99 is stored as a binary approximation, and arithmetic on approximations accumulates error — the classic symptom is a total that renders as $59.96999999999999 before formatting, or worse, a formatted value that rounds the wrong way because the stored number is a hair below the half-cent boundary you can see on paper. The famous case: 2.675 formats to 2.67, not 2.68, because the float is actually 2.67499999....

Integer cents remove the entire category: amounts are exact, addition and subtraction are exact, and formatting is a display decision made once at the boundary (split with divmod, pad the remainder). Decimal is the other honest option when you need fractions of a cent or many decimal places — it does base-10 arithmetic, so 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3, and its quantize step lets you choose the rounding rule explicitly.

The codebase rule is really about where errors are allowed to live. Floats are fine for measurements and statistics, where a relative error of 1e-16 is meaningless. Money is accounted to the cent and reconciled against other systems that did the arithmetic exactly; a one-cent disagreement is a bug report. Keep the value exact upstream, and let the formatter be the only place rounding ever happens.
I'm rendering ratios as percentages with the % format type. What rounding am I actually getting, and where does it bite? Show me a few ratios at different precisions.

arguments.code:
parts = [("A", 1, 3), ("B", 2, 3), ("C", 1, 8), ("D", 3, 8)]
for name, got, total in parts:
    ratio = got / total
    print(f"{name}: {got}/{total} = {ratio:.1%}")
print(f"{1/8:.2%}")
print(f"{0.125:.0%}")

messages.content:
The "%" type multiplies the ratio by 100, appends the sign, and rounds with the same rule as all float formatting: round-half-even applied to the actual binary value. At one decimal, 1/3 renders as 33.3% and 2/3 as 66.7% — the pair sums to 100.0 here, but that is luck, not a guarantee; independently rounded shares often sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is why tables of percentages carry the "may not sum to 100" footnote, or use a largest-remainder adjustment when they must.

The last line is where the policy bites: 0.125 at zero decimals is exactly 12.5 percent, and half-even rounds it to 12%, not the 13% most readers expect from schoolbook rounding. The value is exactly representable in binary, so this is the pure policy showing through, not a representation error. The lesson: the % type gives you a rounding rule whether you chose one or not. If your audience expects half-up (customers, invoices, most business documents), format from Decimal with an explicit quantize; if the numbers are analytical, half-even is fine — but state the policy wherever the numbers are published, because two tools rendering the same ratio can legitimately disagree by a point.
Our ledger export wants accounting-style amounts: negatives in parentheses, everything aligned in a column, positives with a trailing space so the digits line up. Build it from integer cents.

arguments.code:
def acct(cents):
    dollars, rem = divmod(abs(cents), 100)
    s = f"{dollars:,}.{rem:02d}"
    return f"({s})" if cents < 0 else f"{s} "

amounts = [125050, -4200, 987, -1234567, 0]
for a in amounts:
    print(f"{acct(a):>12}")

messages.content:
Accounting format is a convention with three parts: the magnitude formatted normally, negatives wrapped in parentheses instead of a minus sign, and positives padded with a trailing space so a column of mixed values aligns digit-for-digit — the space is the invisible twin of the closing parenthesis. The function builds the magnitude from integer cents with divmod (no float), then branches: parenthesize if negative, append a space if not.

The alignment then comes for free by right-justifying the finished strings in a fixed width — here 12 — which is why the trailing space matters: without it, positive amounts would sit one column left of the parenthesized ones and the eye would read the column as ragged. Zero is treated as positive, rendering as "0.00 " with no parentheses, which matches ledger convention: only actual negatives get the brackets. Two honest limits: this renders one currency with two decimal places — parameterize the decimals if you ever handle zero-decimal currencies — and the parentheses are display only; anything that must be parsed back should travel as the signed integer, never as this string.
What's the difference between decimal places and significant figures when formatting numbers? I keep using .2f for everything, including lab measurements like 0.00012345 and 98765.4.

They answer different questions. Decimal places fix where the value ends relative to the decimal point: .2f always shows exactly two digits after the point, so 0.00012345 becomes 0.00 — every digit of information destroyed — and 98765.4 becomes 98765.40, inventing a trailing zero that claims precision you may not have. The width of the rendered number swings wildly, but the absolute resolution is constant: hundredths.

Significant figures fix how many meaningful digits are shown, wherever they sit: the "g" spec with a precision counts digits from the first nonzero. At three significant figures, 0.00012345 renders as 0.000123 and 98765.4 renders as 98800 (or 9.88e+04 past a magnitude threshold) — both keep three digits of actual information, and the resolution scales with the size of the number.

That is why measurements want significant figures: an instrument's precision is relative, and the rendered digits should claim exactly the digits the measurement supports. Money and counts want decimal places: a cent is a cent at any magnitude, and columns must align. The failure mode of using .2f for everything is the 0.00 above — a real, nonzero measurement rendered as zero. When you see that in a report, the formatter, not the data, is lying.
I tried the g format spec for cleaning up measurement output and got surprised twice: 12345 at .3g came out as 1.23e+04, and 0.00012345 came out as 0.000123. Is g broken?

G is doing exactly what it promises; the surprise is the promise. The precision in a g spec is a count of significant digits — .3g keeps three: 1, 2, and 3. For 12345, three significant digits would be "12300", but g switches to scientific notation whenever the exponent is large relative to the precision (roughly, when the number needs more digits before the decimal point than the precision allows), so you get 1.23e+04. That switch is deliberate: it prevents g from ever printing a long row of trailing zeros that look like measured digits.

For 0.00012345 the same rule keeps three significant digits — 123 — and since the number is small but not tiny enough to trigger scientific notation, you get the plain form 0.000123. The leading zeros are place-holders, not significant digits, so they are free.

Two more g behaviors worth knowing before you adopt it: it strips trailing zeros and a bare decimal point (2.50 at .3g renders as 2.5), which is usually why people reach for it; and the default precision is six significant digits, not six decimal places. If you want guaranteed plain notation with significant-figure discipline, you have to build it yourself — format with g, or use Decimal.normalize with an explicit context — and decide the scientific threshold as a matter of your own house style rather than accepting g's.
I need a humanize function for counts: 999 stays 999, 1234 becomes 1.2k, 3400000 becomes 3.4M. My first version printed "1000.0k" for 999999, which looks broken. Handle the boundaries properly.

The "1000.0k" bug is a rounding boundary, not a scaling bug: 999999 scales to 999.999k, which is correctly below 1000 — but formatting to one decimal rounds the display up to 1000.0, a value the unit can no longer express. The fix is to check the formatted text, not the raw number: if rounding produced exactly "1000.0" and a larger unit exists, promote to 1.0 of the next unit. That is why 999999 renders as 1.0M.

The rest of the boundaries behave as specified: values below 1000 pass through untouched (999 stays "999", so small counts never gain a fake decimal), 1000 becomes 1.0k, and 999949 scales to 999.949k, which rounds down to 999.9k without promotion. Notice the function is honest about precision: one decimal means 1234 and 1249 both render as 1.2k — acceptable for a dashboard count, unacceptable anywhere the exact value matters. Humanizing is a lossy display choice; keep the true integer behind it (a tooltip, a title attribute, the underlying data) so the rounded text is never the only record of the number.
Our survey report shows each option's share to one decimal place, and the column must sum to exactly 100.0. Rounding each share independently gives me 99.9 or 100.1. Fix it properly.

The standard fix is the largest remainder method, and it works in integer units so the result is exact. Work in tenths of a percent: each share is votes/total*1000 tenths. Truncate each to a whole number of tenths — that undershoots, here by 2 tenths (the bases sum to 998 of 1000). Then hand the missing tenths, one each, to the shares with the largest discarded remainders: C discarded .919 of a tenth and B discarded .727, so they round up, while A (.141) and D (.212) stay truncated.

The printed column — 41.4, 27.3, 19.2, 12.1 — now sums to exactly 100.0, and every value is within one tenth of its true share, which is provably the best a one-decimal display can do. Two disciplines make this production-worthy: do the arithmetic on integers (tenths) rather than floats, so the final sum is exact by construction rather than by luck; and apply the method at render time only — the stored data stays as raw counts, because adjusted percentages cannot be un-adjusted by the next person who needs two decimals. This is the same apportionment mathematics used for parliamentary seats, which is a good reminder that "the percentages don't add up" is a solved problem with a name.

Our dashboard prints sensor values with twelve decimal places because that's what the float gives us: 21.500000000004 °C. The sensor is accurate to about half a degree. How much precision should the display actually show?

One decimal at most, and arguably none. Displayed precision is a claim about knowledge: every digit you print asserts "this digit means something." Twelve decimals claim you know the temperature to a trillionth of a degree, from a sensor that is honest to half a degree. Readers — especially engineers scanning quickly — trust the digits they see, so false precision is not harmless decoration; it is misinformation that also makes the real signal harder to read, because the meaningful variation drowns in noise digits that jitter between refreshes.

The rule: render one digit beyond the precision you actually trust, at most. A sensor accurate to ±0.5 °C earns "21.5" (the tenths digit is mostly real, the hundredths would be fiction). A value computed from exact inputs — counts, money — is the opposite case and can carry full precision, because there the digits are exact by construction.

Two practical corollaries. First, round at render, never in the stored data: the raw readings stay full-precision for anyone who later averages or audits them. Second, make the choice in one formatting helper per quantity, not per screen — if the temperature is formatted in six places, it will eventually appear with six different precisions, and two screenshots of the same moment will disagree. Consistency is part of the claim too.
The comma grouping in f"{n:,}" — is that my system's locale? We're deploying on servers in three countries and I need the output to be predictable.

No — and that predictability is the point. The "," in a format spec is a fixed convention, not a locale lookup: it always groups by thousands with commas, and the decimal point is always ".", regardless of the server's country, environment variables, or installed locales. The "_" variant is likewise fixed. Your three servers will produce byte-identical output, which is exactly what you want for logs, exports, and anything a test might compare.

Python does have a locale-aware option: the "n" type in a format spec, f"{n:n}", uses the current C locale's grouping — which on most servers is the default "C" locale and groups nothing at all, unless something calls locale.setlocale. That global, process-wide, thread-unsafe switch is why experienced teams avoid "n" and the locale module for output formatting: the same binary can render differently because an unrelated library flipped a global.

If you genuinely need per-country presentation — 1.234.567,89 for a German invoice — do it explicitly at the presentation layer with a formatting function chosen by the target audience (or a library like Babel), with the locale passed as a value, not read from the environment. Deterministic-by-default, localized-by-explicit-choice is the only combination that survives deployment.
I'm printing a plain-text table and hardcoding column widths, so it breaks whenever longer data shows up. How do I derive the widths from the data itself and align text left, numbers right?

arguments.code:
rows = [
    ("name", "qty", "price"),
    ("apples", "7", "0.65"),
    ("pears", "120", "1.20"),
    ("dragon fruit", "3", "4.75"),
]
widths = [max(len(r[i]) for r in rows) for i in range(3)]
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r[0]:<{widths[0]}}  {r[1]:>{widths[1]}}  {r[2]:>{widths[2]}}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
name          qty  price
apples          7   0.65
pears         120   1.20
dragon fruit    3   4.75

Measure the data, then format with the measurements. The widths list takes, for each column index, the length of the longest cell in that column — including the header row, which is why the header is just row zero of the data rather than a special case. "dragon fruit" sets column one to 12, "120" sets column two to 3. The print then uses nested format specs: the width is a variable substituted into the spec, with "<" for the text column and ">" for the numeric ones.

Right-aligning numbers is not cosmetic: it lines up units and decimal places so magnitudes compare at a glance, which is the entire reason the table exists. Two honest limits to know. This measures length in characters, so a cell containing wide CJK characters or combining marks will misalign visually — len() is not display width. And the two-space gutter between columns is a constant here; make it part of the layout if your widths get tight. The pattern to keep is: one pass to measure, one pass to render, widths never typed by hand — when the data grows, the table grows correctly instead of silently clipping.
Some rows in my data have missing cells and one has an extra. My table printer either crashes or silently misaligns everything after the short row. How should I handle ragged rows?

First, see the raggedness: the audit loop prints each row's length before you commit to a policy — 3, 2, 3. Only then decide what a missing cell means. Here the policy is "missing means not applicable," rendered as a dash: each row is padded with placeholders up to the column count and sliced to exactly that count, so every printed row has the same shape and the columns after the gap stay in their lanes.

But be honest about what padding does: it makes a data problem invisible. If the short row is short because an upstream parser dropped a field, the dash launders that bug into a plausible-looking table, and the misalignment you feared is replaced by something worse — wrong values in right-looking columns. The alternative policies are to reject the batch (raise on any row whose length differs, with the row index in the message) or to render the dash and also count and report how many cells were padded. Production code usually wants the third option: display resilience plus a visible count. What it never wants is the silent version, where zip() quietly truncates every row to the shortest and the table "works" while dropping data.
Why does my hand-rolled table code keep breaking? I join values with tabs, or pad names to 15 characters with ljust, and it looks fine until it suddenly doesn't.

Because both approaches smuggle in an assumption about the data, and the data eventually breaks it. Tab-joining assumes the terminal or the reader will land tabs on the same stops you imagined — tab stops are the viewer's setting, not yours, so the same file aligns on one machine and staircases on another. Worse, a value that itself contains a tab or newline doesn't just misalign the row, it manufactures extra columns and rows.

Fixed-width padding assumes every value fits the width you picked: ljust(15) does nothing at all to a 20-character name — it doesn't truncate, it just returns the longer string — so one long value pushes every later column sideways for that row only, which is the "looks fine until it doesn't" pattern exactly.

Two deeper traps sit under both. Length is not width: len() counts characters, but terminals render East Asian wide characters in two cells and combining characters in zero, so even perfectly padded strings can misalign. And numbers padded as text align their left edges, while readers compare numbers by their right edges and decimal points.

The durable fix is to measure the actual data (maximum cell length per column), format with explicit alignment per column type, and decide a truncation policy for over-long values before they arrive — not to pick a constant and hope.

Second, len() counts characters, not terminal cells: a name with wide CJK characters measures 6 but renders 12 cells wide, and a combining accent measures 2 but renders 1. If your table must align on a real terminal with international data, measure with a display-width function (wcwidth) and truncate by cells, not by len(). When I generate a table, should I produce fixed-width aligned columns or a delimited format like CSV/TSV? I keep going back and forth.

Decide by naming the consumer. If a human reads it in a terminal, an email, or a report, fixed-width aligned columns are the right output: magnitudes line up, scanning is fast, and the layout itself carries meaning. If anything else — a spreadsheet, a parser, another program — consumes it, produce a delimited format and never let a human-facing concern (alignment, padding, truncation) anywhere near it.

The failure mode is mixing the two: a "CSV" padded with spaces for beauty breaks naive parsers and some strict ones; a fixed-width file fed to a program forces it to guess column boundaries and breaks the first time a value outgrows its width. They also age differently: delimited output is stable when data changes shape, while fixed-width must re-measure every run.

Practical corollaries. Never truncate or round for display in machine output — the delimited file carries full values, the human table may summarize. Never make the human table the system's record: if someone later needs the data, regenerate the delimited form from the source, don't scrape the pretty one. And if both audiences exist, write two renderers over the same computed rows — the shared part is the data and the aggregates, the rendering is the cheap part. One dataset, two honest renderings, zero hybrids.
How should headers and separator rows work in a generated fixed-width table? Mine look off: the header is left-aligned over right-aligned numbers and the dashes never match the columns.

Treat the header and separator as rows rendered by the same machinery as the data, with two deliberate differences. First, the header's alignment is a choice per column, not a copy of the data's: for numeric columns, right-aligning the header with the numbers keeps the column visually unified, while centering short headers ("qty") over wide right-aligned columns often reads best. What looks broken is the accidental version — headers defaulting to left because they were printed by a separate, simpler line of code. Route them through the same width table so only the alignment flag differs.

Second, the separator row should be generated from the widths, not typed: one run of dashes per column, exactly the column's width, joined by the same gutter as every other row. A hand-typed "--------" line matches only until the data changes the widths, and then it silently disagrees with every row it separates. Generate it: "  ".join("-" * w for w in widths) can never drift.

The underlying principle is that a table is one layout computed once — widths, gutters, alignments — and every line (title excepted) is a projection of that layout. The moment any line is formatted by its own ad-hoc code, it becomes a future inconsistency with a date on it.
I generate TSV files by joining fields with tabs. A user pasted a product description containing tabs and a line break, and now the file has phantom columns and rows. Is TSV just fragile?

TSV is fragile in a specific way: unlike CSV it has no standard quoting mechanism. CSV defines exactly how to wrap a field containing commas, quotes, or newlines; TSV's convention is simply that fields may not contain tabs or newlines at all. So your generator didn't have a bug in the joining — it had missing input discipline: the format makes a promise ("no tabs, no newlines in values") that free-text data never signed.

You have three honest options. Sanitize at generation: replace tabs and newlines in values with spaces. This keeps TSV but is lossy — the original text is altered, which is fine for a display export and not fine for a data exchange. Switch formats: if the data is arbitrary user text, use CSV with its quoting rules (and a real csv module), or JSON Lines, which escapes control characters by construction. Or keep TSV and validate: reject or flag values containing the forbidden characters, so the corruption becomes a visible error at write time instead of a silent one at read time.

What not to do is invent a private escaping (backslash-t, say) and keep calling it TSV — the next tool reads it as literal backslashes and your phantom columns become phantom data. Every simple format is a contract about what values may contain; the generator's job is to enforce the contract or pick a format whose contract the data can actually keep.

What's the practical difference between Template.substitute and Template.safe_substitute? Our notification templates sometimes lack a value at send time.

messages.content:
Hello Ana, your order A-17 ships Friday.
Hello Ana, your order A-17 ships $when.
KeyError: 'when'

Same template, two failure philosophies. substitute is strict: render with the full mapping and you get the finished sentence; render with "when" missing and it raises KeyError: 'when' before producing anything. safe_substitute is lenient: with the same partial mapping it produces the message anyway, leaving the literal text "$when" in place where the value should have gone.

Which one you want depends on which failure is worse. For a shipping notification, strict is usually right: a KeyError in your logs is visible and fixable, while a customer receiving "your order ships $when" is a silent embarrassment that no alarm will ever report — safe_substitute converts a programming error into user-facing garbage. The legitimate uses of safe_substitute are narrow: layered rendering, where a second pass will fill the remaining placeholders, or best-effort previews. Note also that both methods raise ValueError on a malformed template (a lone "$" with no valid placeholder after it), because that is a template bug, not a data gap. Choose per template, deliberately, and let strict be the default.

safe: Hi ana, you wrote: Hi {user}, psst: {secret}

They are right, and the first line is the proof. When user-controlled text is the template, every placeholder in it is resolved against your context: the user typed {secret} — a key you never intended to offer — and .format happily substituted your token into their message. The placeholder list you documented ({user}) is not a boundary; the boundary is whatever keys and attributes the format machinery can reach, and field access goes further than keys: {user.__class__} style attribute traversal is the classic escalation from data leak to object-graph exploration.

The second line is the correct architecture. Your template is a fixed string you wrote — "Hi {user}, you wrote: {note}" — and the user's text enters strictly as a value. As a value it is inert: its braces are just characters, printed literally, never interpreted. The rule generalizes beyond str.format: a template is code. Code comes from developers, is reviewed, and is trusted; data comes from users and is rendered. Any design where user input becomes the format string — templates from a database edited by non-developers, "personalization" that formats the customer's own text — has the same hole, whatever the library. If users genuinely need placeholders, offer a tiny allow-listed syntax of your own and substitute by hand.
We let the marketing team edit email templates stored in our database. The templates use str.format placeholders. Is there anything about that I should be more careful about?

Yes: a str.format template is not inert text, it is a small program that runs against whatever object graph you hand it. Field names can traverse attributes and indexes — {order.customer.email} walks objects, {config[api_key]} indexes mappings — and the dunder attributes are reachable from almost anywhere, which is the well-known path from a format string to reading class internals. The moment non-developers can edit templates, they can write placeholders you never reviewed, resolving against everything in your render context.

Three controls, in increasing strength. First, shrink the context: pass a flat dict of exactly the scalars the template may use, never objects with attributes worth walking. That reduces the blast radius but does not remove it, because a plain string value still exposes its class through attribute access.

Second, switch the engine: string.Template's $name syntax substitutes mapping keys only — no attribute traversal, no indexing, no format specs. It was designed for exactly this "template as data" job, and its poverty is the feature.

Third, treat stored templates like code operationally: version them, review changes, and render-test them in CI against a sample context so a bad placeholder fails a build instead of a campaign. The principle to keep: whoever can write the template can execute the template. Grant that power at the level the engine actually enforces, not the level the placeholder examples suggest.

attribute: "><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

The hostile name is built to break out: its leading double-quote closes an attribute, and the tag with an onerror handler is the payload. Escaping converts the structural characters into entities so the browser treats them as text, never markup. The two lines show why the destination decides the settings. With quote=False, only &, <, and > are escaped — enough for a text node, where quotes are ordinary characters; the tag is neutralized because its angle brackets became < and >. But that same output placed inside a double-quoted attribute is still exploitable: the name's own " survives and terminates the attribute early. With quote=True (the default), double quotes become " and single quotes ', so the value cannot break out of either quoting style. The general rule: escaping is not a property of the data, it is a property of the context the data is entering. The same name needs different treatment in a text node, an attribute, a URL, or a script block — and no single "sanitize" call covers all four. Escape at the point of insertion, with the settings for that exact context; frameworks that auto-escape template values are doing precisely this, which is why bypassing them with a "safe" flag deserves the scrutiny it gets in review.

I wrote one sanitize() function that strips <, >, quotes, semicolons, and backslashes, and I run all user input through it before using it anywhere — HTML, SQL, file paths, shell commands. My reviewer says this is wrong. Why?

Because "dangerous character" is not a property of a character; it is a property of a character in a context. A semicolon is structural in SQL and shell, harmless in HTML text. A quote ends an attribute in HTML, a string in SQL, and is ordinary punctuation in a paragraph. Your single function therefore fails in both directions at once: it corrupts legitimate data everywhere (nobody named O'Brien can register, no product description can contain a quote), while still missing context-specific attacks — stripping angle brackets does nothing for a value placed in an unquoted HTML attribute, a URL parameter, or a JavaScript string.

Worse, it sanitizes at the wrong moment. Input-time mangling destroys the data for every future use, including the ones where it was perfectly safe — the name in a plain-text email now carries the damage done for HTML's sake. The correct architecture is the opposite: store the value exactly as given, and escape (or better, parameterize) at each point of use, with the mechanism that context provides. HTML gets html.escape or a template engine's auto-escaping at render. SQL gets bound parameters, which are not escaping at all — the value never becomes syntax. Shell gets argument arrays instead of a command string. Paths get resolved and checked against the allowed root.

One honest value, many context-correct exits. A universal sanitizer feels like defense in depth; it is actually data corruption in depth, with holes exactly where the contexts differ.
I want layered template contexts: site-wide defaults, per-product overrides, and per-send values on top, without merging dicts by hand at every call site. Is there a clean way?

Yes — format_map accepts any mapping, and collections.ChainMap is a mapping built for exactly this layering. ChainMap(per_send, per_product, site_defaults) looks keys up through its layers in order and returns the first hit, so a per-send value shadows the product override, which shadows the default, while keys defined only in the defaults resolve transparently. The template renders with template.format_map(chain) and never knows the layering exists.

This beats manual merging for two reasons. The merge {**defaults, **product, **send} copies eagerly and throws away the provenance — six months later nobody can tell whether a value came from the site defaults or a one-off send. The ChainMap keeps the layers distinct and inspectable (chain.maps is the list), so "why did this email say that?" has an answer. And because lookups are live views, updating a default updates every render that falls through to it, with no re-merge step to forget.

Two cautions. Writes go to the first map only, which is usually what you want (per-send tweaks never leak into defaults), but code that mutates the chain expecting to edit a default will confuse you. And a key missing from every layer still raises KeyError — layering organizes values, it does not forgive their absence. Pair it with a strict substitute at send time and a validation pass over the template's field list at load time, and the three layers stay both flexible and safe.
F-strings, str.format templates, string.Template, or a full template engine — how do I pick for a given job?

Ask three questions: who writes the template, when is it rendered, and how much logic does it need?

F-strings: the developer writes it, it renders on the spot, and the "logic" is just expressions. Log lines you are about to print, error messages, CLI output, debug prints. The moment the wording must outlive the code or be edited without a deploy, f-strings are disqualified — they cannot be stored as data.

str.format / format_map: the developer writes it, but rendering happens later or elsewhere with supplied values — message templates in a config file, a report skeleton filled by different callers. You get named fields, format specs, and multiple renders from one string. You also get a template that can traverse attributes, so the author must be trusted like a developer.

string.Template: the author is not fully trusted, or the values are a flat mapping and $name is all you need. Notification wording edited by operations, user-facing copy in a database. Its weakness — no specs, no traversal — is precisely its safety.

A full engine (Jinja2 and friends): the template needs real presentation logic — loops over line items, conditionals, inheritance between a base layout and variants — typically for HTML or documents. That power is justified when the document structure itself is the work; it is overkill, and extra attack surface, for a two-line notification.

The common mistake is reaching up the ladder out of habit (an engine for a greeting) or staying at the bottom out of familiarity (f-strings pasted into a config file, where they can never work). Match the tool to who writes, when it renders, and how much logic is honest.

Yes — format_map looks keys up on the mapping you give it, and a dict subclass with __missing__ controls what "absent" means. Here __missing__ returns the placeholder text itself, "{unread}", so the render completes: present keys substitute normally ("ana", 5), and the missing one passes through visibly in a form a second render pass can still resolve, or a human reviewer can spot in a preview.

Keep the discipline strict, though: this pattern deliberately defers an error, so use it only where a later stage genuinely re-renders or reviews — in a final send path, a missing value should raise, because "{unread}" in a customer's inbox is the same embarrassment as "$unread", just in your house style. A good compromise is SafeDict during composition and a final validation pass that asserts no "{...}" placeholders survive in finished output, turning silent gaps into one clear failure at the boundary.
Our logging style guide bans f-strings in log calls and insists on logger.info("user %s logged in", user). It feels old-fashioned. Is there a real reason?

There are two real reasons, and neither is nostalgia. The first is cost: an f-string is evaluated when the line executes, whether or not any handler will emit the record. In a hot loop, logger.debug(f"state: {expensive_render()}") pays the formatting cost a million times for a message nobody reads at the production level. The %-style call passes the template and the arguments separately; the logging module formats only if the record actually passes the level filter. You are not saving microseconds of string building in the common case — you are avoiding work whose result is provably discarded.

The second reason is failure isolation. If formatting raises — a __format__ bug, a value whose repr explodes — inside an f-string, the exception replaces your log line and can break the code path you were trying to observe. With deferred args, the logging module catches formatting errors and still emits a record (with a traceback about the formatting failure), so the observability tool cannot take down the observed system.

The honest limits: for info-and-above calls in cold paths, the cost argument is negligible, and many teams allow f-strings there for readability; structured logging changes the calculus again, since the fields travel as data either way. But in libraries and hot paths, the guide is right: pass the template and the values, and let the framework decide whether the text is ever born.

By default, textwrap guarantees the width: a word longer than 24 columns is hard-split mid-word and used to fill the current line exactly, with the remainder flowing onto the next line. No output line exceeds the width, but the 28-letter word is sawn apart with no hyphen or apology.

With break_long_words=False the guarantee flips: words are never split, so the long word gets a line to itself and that line overflows to its full 28 characters while every other line respects the width. Neither is wrong — they serve different readers. Splitting is right for fixed containers (a terminal pane, a label, a table cell) where overflow corrupts the layout around the text. Not splitting is right for prose a human reads, where a mangled word is worse than one long line — and for anything containing URLs or identifiers, where a split point invites copy errors.

Know which guarantee your caller needs before you wrap: if the text goes into a fixed-width slot in a larger layout, the default protects the layout; if it goes to a person, prefer whole words and let one line run long.     def greet():
        print("hello")
"""
print("dedented:")
print(textwrap.dedent(snippet).strip())
print("indented:")
print(textwrap.indent(textwrap.dedent(snippet).strip(), "    "))

messages.content:
The snippet starts life uniformly over-indented because it was copied out of a nested context. textwrap.dedent removes the longest common leading whitespace from every line: here four spaces come off all lines, so "def greet():" lands at column zero while its body keeps its relative four-space indent — dedent normalizes the block without touching the internal structure. The .strip() is there because the triple-quoted source carries a leading and trailing newline that are artifacts of how the literal was written, not content.

textwrap.indent is the exact inverse operation: it prepends a prefix to every line, re-embedding the now-clean block at a chosen depth in generated code — here four spaces, simulating the block nested inside a function of the generated file. The pair is the standard pipeline for code generation: capture at whatever indentation the source had, dedent to canonical zero, then indent to the target depth. Two cautions: dedent is defeated by a single line with less indentation than the rest (often a stray unindented line), because the common prefix collapses to that line's depth; and tabs and spaces are different characters to both functions, so mixed-indentation input must be expanded first. Normalize whitespace at capture time and generation stays boring.
Beyond width, what are the textwrap knobs I should actually know about? My wrapped output sometimes eats my tabs and collapses spacing in ways I didn't ask for.

Four knobs explain nearly all surprises. expand_tabs (default True) converts tabs to spaces before wrapping — usually welcome, but it means a tab-indented structure comes out space-indented with the tab stops textwrap chose. replace_whitespace (default True) then converts every remaining whitespace character — newlines included — into plain spaces, which is why fill() flattens a multi-paragraph string into one stream; if your input has meaningful line breaks, wrap paragraph by paragraph instead. drop_whitespace (default True) removes whitespace at line starts and ends, including swallowing the space at a wrap point; turn it off when leading spaces are indentation you intend to keep.

The remaining two govern breaking: break_long_words (default True) hard-splits words longer than the width, and break_on_hyphens (default True) allows breaks after hyphens in compound words — and also inside hyphenated paths and identifiers, which is why wrapped file paths sometimes split at a dash.

The pattern behind the defaults: textwrap assumes it is reformatting prose for a fresh layout, so it normalizes whitespace aggressively. When your text is not prose — code, preformatted blocks, anything with meaningful spacing — either bypass fill and use wrap on individual paragraphs with the knobs set conservatively, or reach for indent/dedent, which are the textwrap tools that promise to preserve structure.

Layer two assembles: collect the present parts in order — header, paragraphs, attachments — and join with exactly one blank line between them, letting join own the separators so the optional section can vanish without leaving a gap. Parts, assembly, termination: keep those three apart and a memo generator stays a page of boring, correct code.
Python formatted 2.5 as "2" but 3.5 as "4" at zero decimals. That looks like a bug — sometimes it rounds down on a half, sometimes up. Explain what's happening.

It is a rule, not a bug: round-half-even, also called bankers' rounding. When the discarded part is exactly half, the result is whichever neighbor is even. 2.5 sits between 2 and 3, and 2 is even, so it rounds down; 3.5 sits between 3 and 4, and 4 is even, so it rounds up; 4.5 confirms the pattern by going to 4. The second line shows the same rule at two decimals: 0.125 becomes 0.12 (2 is even) and 0.375 becomes 0.38 (8 is even).

Why would anyone choose this? Because always rounding halves up introduces a systematic upward bias: over many roundings — interest calculations, statistical aggregates — the errors accumulate in one direction. Half-even makes half the halves go up and half down, so the bias cancels in aggregate. It is the default in IEEE 754 arithmetic and in Python's round() and float formatting alike.

Two qualifications. These examples are exactly representable in binary, so the true half-even rule is what you see; a decimal like 2.675 is not exactly representable, and its float is slightly less than the written value, so it rounds down for a different reason entirely (that is the representation trap, not the policy). And if your domain expects half-up — most customers and many regulations do — float formatting will never give it to you; that requires Decimal with an explicit rounding mode.

Python's repr deliberately shows the shortest string that round-trips to the same double, so you see the 4. The arithmetic did nothing wrong by floating-point standards; the display made a promise the value can't keep.

The wrong fixes are the tempting ones: rounding the stored total (you have now corrupted data to please a display), or truncating the string (which breaks on the next magnitude). The right fix is to format at the boundary with the precision the quantity actually has: f"{total:.2f}" renders 0.30, because two decimals is what a sum of tenths means in this UI. Formatting rounds the value for presentation and leaves the stored double untouched for anyone who needs it.

Know the boundary of this advice: if the values are money, the correct fix is upstream — integer cents or Decimal — because display rounding will eventually disagree with a reconciliation done exactly. For measured or computed floats, format-at-display is the whole answer, and the number of decimals is a statement about the quantity's real precision, not a cosmetic choice.

Python's round() and float formatting use round-half-even: a value exactly halfway goes to the even neighbor, so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. The policy exists to cancel bias over many roundings. Your billing spec uses round-half-up (technically half-away-from-zero for negatives): every exact half goes up in magnitude, so 2.5 becomes 3. Neither is a bug; they are different contracts, and financial and consumer-facing documents overwhelmingly specify half-up because it matches what people learned in school and what auditors expect.

Getting half-up reliably requires Decimal, for two reasons. First, Decimal("2.5") is exactly two and a half — a float literal 2.5 happens to be exact too, but a float like 2.675 is not the value written, and no rounding mode can recover intent from a value that is already off. Construct Decimals from strings or integers, never from floats. Second, Decimal.quantize takes the policy explicitly: Decimal("2.5").quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP) is 3, while the same quantize with ROUND_HALF_EVEN is 2.

The process lesson matters as much as the mechanism: the rounding rule is part of the specification of any money output, on the same level as the tax rate. And quantize on a value with more precision than the target is the one and only place rounding should occur in a money pipeline: compute exactly, quantize once at the end, format the quantized Decimal — it will render with exactly the scale you set.

Second, write the helper as the single owner of the whole decision: fmt_money(cents) or fmt_amount(decimal) that internally does the quantize and the format, so no caller can perform half the policy. If callers can still reach the raw value and format it themselves, you have five copies again, one of them shared.

Third, give the helper tests that encode the policy's edge cases: the halfway value under your rounding mode, zero, a negative, a value needing grouping, the smallest unit. These tests are the spec made executable — when the policy is questioned in six months, they are the documentation that answers.

Fourth, migrate the call sites and delete the copies, all of them, including the "temporary" one in the export script. A helper that coexists with surviving copies is just the newest copy. The payoff is not tidiness; it is that the next policy change — a new rounding rule, a currency with zero decimals — becomes a one-function change with tests, instead of an archaeological expedition.

A report showed a tax rate of 1700%. The stored value was 0.17. Somewhere a percentage got scaled twice. How do I structure formatting so this class of bug can't happen?

Name the unit in the value's identity and let exactly one place do the scaling. The bug's anatomy: the value 0.17 is a ratio. One layer formatted it with the % type, which multiplies by 100 (17%). Another layer, written by someone who thought the value was "17 meaning percent," multiplied again before handing it over — 1700%. Both layers were locally reasonable; the contract between them was nowhere written down.

The structural defenses: store ratios as ratios everywhere (0.17), and let the % format spec be the only multiplication by 100 in the codebase — a value should never be pre-scaled "for display" before reaching the formatter, because the next formatter cannot tell a ratio from a pre-scaled number by looking at it. Where a value genuinely is in percent units (some APIs deliver 17 meaning 17%), convert it to a ratio at the ingestion boundary and name it accordingly inside your system.

Naming is the cheap half of the defense: rate_ratio vs rate_percent as variable and column names make the wrong hand-off visible in review. The other half is a boundary test: render the known rate through the real pipeline and assert the output string "17%" — the class of bug you described survives unit tests of each layer and dies instantly in an end-to-end render test. Scaling is formatting; formatting happens once, at the boundary; the test proves it.
I need to print floats across a huge range — millions, and millionths — in a compact summary. Show me how the g and e specs behave on the same values, and where each one goes wrong.

Read the three columns as three contracts. The g column (.3g, three significant digits) adapts its notation: 1234567 becomes 1.23e+06 because plain notation would need seven digits, 0.00001234 becomes 1.23e-05, and 987.654 becomes 988 — plain, because three significant digits fit. The e column (.2e) is scientific always: mantissa with two decimals and an exponent, uniform and sortable-looking across any range, at the cost of making everyday magnitudes (988 as 9.88e+02) feel like laboratory output.

The third column is the cautionary tale: .2f is a fixed decimal-places contract applied to values it cannot serve. The million prints in full (fine but wide), and 0.00001234 prints as 0.00 — a real, nonzero measurement rendered as zero, the single most dangerous output a formatter can produce, because nothing about it looks wrong. The rule that emerges: choose the spec by the range of the quantity, not by habit. Fixed decimals for quantities near unit scale (money, percentages), g for compact summaries across ranges, e when the audience is technical and the range is extreme. And whatever you choose, scan the rendered output for the two failure shapes — a nonzero value shown as 0.00, and a rounded value shown with more certainty than the measurement holds.
You keep saying "format from an exact source." Practically, what does that mean for a pipeline where values arrive as JSON numbers, get summed, taxed, discounted, and finally printed on an invoice?

It means the type of the value is decided at the system's edge, and floats are refused entry for anything that must be exact. A JSON number like 19.99 arrives as text; the standard parser hands you a float, and from that instant the value is an approximation that no downstream care can undo. Parse with parse_float=Decimal (json supports it directly) and the number that enters is exactly 19.99. Sums, tax multiplications, and discounts then run in Decimal arithmetic — exact for addition and multiplication at sane scales, with division the one operation to watch (give the context enough precision and quantize deliberately at defined points, typically per-line or per-invoice, per your spec).

"Format from an exact source" is the end of that chain: because the value reaching the formatter is exact, the single quantize at print time is the only rounding in the pipeline, it applies your stated policy, and two systems fed the same inputs produce byte-identical invoices. The float version of the same pipeline rounds a little at every operation, in ways that depend on operation order — which is why float pipelines produce the one-cent disagreements that nobody can reproduce from the spec.

Where floats remain legitimate: anything measured rather than defined — sensor readings, statistics, ML scores — where the input itself is approximate and exactness is a fiction. The discipline is per-quantity, not per-codebase: money, counts, rates from a contract, and thresholds from a spec travel exactly; measurements travel as floats; and the formatter treats each accordingly. The invoice is exact because every stage refused to be approximate.

The malign face is the same mechanism aimed deliberately: a value crafted to close the literal and append its own SQL is the classic injection attack, and it works precisely because the database cannot distinguish your syntax from the value's contents once they are concatenated into one string.

A teammate says they'll "just escape the quotes" in values before building SQL strings, instead of using parameterized queries. Why do we insist parameterization is different from escaping?

Because they defend at different layers, and only one of them can be complete. Escaping is a promise about characters: "I have neutralized every character that could be special." That promise has to hold for every value, every encoding, and every context the string passes through — and its history is a trail of bypasses: a character the escaper forgot, a multibyte encoding that smuggles a quote past a byte-oriented check, a numeric field where the attacker needs no quote at all (a value of "1 OR 1=1" in an unquoted slot sails through quote-escaping untouched). Each failure is silent and total.

Parameterization makes no promise about characters because the value never becomes part of the query text. The SQL is parsed once, with placeholders; values are bound afterward as typed data and can only ever be compared or stored, never executed. There is no character that breaks out, because there is no string to break out of — the same structural reason values passed to a template as data cannot inject placeholders.

Two corollaries worth stating in review. First, placeholders bind values, not identifiers: table and column names cannot be parameterized, so dynamic identifiers need a strict allow-list of your own — a different mechanism for a different slot. Second, "the ORM handles it" is true only while you stay in its query builder; the raw-SQL escape hatch reopens the hole, which is why raw SQL in a codebase deserves the scrutiny of a small audit. Escaping is hygiene; parameterization is architecture. Only one of those words belongs in a security review.

Every format I generate — CSV, JSON, config files, query strings — I currently build by concatenating strings. It mostly works. What's the argument for always using the format's own writer?

The argument is that "mostly works" is a property of your current data, not of your code, and data changes without asking. Every text format has structural characters and a rule for neutralizing them inside values: CSV quotes fields containing commas, quotes, or newlines and doubles internal quotes; JSON escapes quotes, backslashes, and control characters and has opinions about numbers; a query string percent-encodes &, =, and spaces; an INI file has comment characters and key separators. Concatenation knows none of this. It produces correct output exactly when no value contains a structural character — a bet that fails the day a customer is named O'Brien, a note contains a newline, or a search term contains an ampersand, and fails silently, as corrupt files and broken queries rather than errors.

The format's writer — csv.writer, json.dumps, configparser, urlencode — encodes the whole rulebook, including the edge cases you have not met yet: the field that is exactly a quote, the string with a trailing backslash, the None that must become an empty field or a null. It also localizes change: when the consumer turns out to need a different delimiter or line terminator, the writer takes a parameter and your forty concatenation sites take a sed.

The cost is one import and slightly less "transparent" code. The failure it prevents is the worst kind in generated artifacts: output that looks right, parses wrong, and is discovered by the consumer. Build text by hand only when the format has no structural characters at all — and count the formats you use that qualify. It is a short list.

I generate .env files from a settings dict. Values with spaces or # in them break when the file is loaded. What quoting rules should the generator follow?

A .env line is KEY=value, and the value runs to the end of the line — but two characters are structural for most loaders: a "#" begins a comment when preceded by whitespace (so a password containing " #" silently truncates), and an unquoted value with spaces may be split or rejected by stricter parsers (the format is a convention, not a standard, and loaders differ — shell sourcing, python-dotenv, and Docker's env_file each have their own exact rules). The generator's safe rule: quote any value that contains a space, a #, a quote, or leading/trailing whitespace, using double quotes, and escape the two characters that are special inside double quotes for your target loader — the double quote itself and, for dotenv-style loaders, the dollar sign if variable expansion is enabled.

Also decide the boring cases deliberately: an empty value is KEY= (present but empty), which is not the same as omitting the key — loaders and the programs reading them distinguish unset from empty, and your generator should preserve the distinction the settings dict carries. Non-string values get rendered canonically (True as "true" if that is what the consumer expects — check, because the consumer is the contract).

And a boundary note: .env files hold secrets. A generator that writes them should also set restrictive permissions on the file it creates and keep the values out of its own logs. The quoting rules keep the file parseable; the handling rules keep it from leaking while it sits there.
Generated files in our repo keep showing diffs when "nothing changed" — key order flips, rows shuffle. Why does deterministic output matter and how do I get it?

A generated file that changes bytes without a change in meaning destroys the signal of every tool built on comparison: diffs in review become noise nobody reads, golden-file tests fail randomly and get disabled, caches and content hashes invalidate for no reason, and two environments producing "the same" artifact can no longer be verified equal. Deterministic output — same input, byte-identical output, every run, every machine — turns all of those back on.

The nondeterminism in generated text almost always comes from a short list of sources. Iteration order of sets (and dicts built from sets): Python set order depends on hash values, and string hashing is randomized per process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is pinned, so a set of keys can serialize in a different order on every run — sort keys and rows at generation time. Data structure construction order: a dict assembled from unordered query results inherits the database's mood — impose ORDER BY or sort in the generator. Embedded environment data: timestamps, hostnames, absolute paths, version strings of the generator itself — pin them, parameterize them, or leave them out of the compared artifact. And float formatting of values computed in different orders, which can differ in the last bit.

The working rule: at generation time, sort everything sortable, format everything explicitly, and include nothing you did not decide to include. Then test it the way the property states: run the generator twice in separate processes and diff the outputs. If they differ, the generator — not the test — is wrong.

Your search term "fish & chips" joined naively produces "q=fish & chips&page=2", which the server parses as three parameters — q="fish ", an empty " chips" key, and page — the value's & is indistinguishable from the separator's. urlencode percent-encodes the structural characters inside values (and keys): the same input becomes "q=fish+%26+chips&page=2", where %26 is unambiguously data. An "=" inside a value gets the same treatment (%3D), as do other reserved characters.

Three details complete the picture. urlencode takes a mapping or a list of pairs — use the list form when a key legitimately repeats (tag=a&tag=b), since a dict cannot hold both. Its quote_via defaults to quote_plus, which encodes spaces as "+", correct for query strings in forms; for other URL components, quote with safe="" is the stricter tool. And encoding is per-component: you encode values, then join — never build the string and encode the whole thing afterward, which would encode your own separators too and produce one giant unreadable value.

This is the same lesson as CSV and SQL wearing URL clothes: the format has structural characters, values will eventually contain them, and the standard library already owns the rulebook. The day a value contains the separator is not bad luck; it is the schedule.

Store the golden file next to the test, in version control, as a first-class artifact.
We started keeping golden files for our generated reports. Twice now someone "fixed" a failing test by regenerating the golden file without looking. How do we keep golden testing honest?

By treating the golden file as a specification that happens to be stored as output, and its regeneration as a change that requires the same scrutiny as the code. The mechanics are easy — a --update flag on the test runner — so the discipline has to be social and structural.

Structurally: make regeneration a separate, visible step, never a side effect of running the tests. Tests only compare; a distinct command updates. Keep golden files in version control alongside the tests so every regeneration appears in the same pull request as the code change that caused it, and require the diff of the golden file to be reviewed line by line — the reviewer asks "is each changed line the change we intended?" That question is unanswerable when the diff is 400 lines of churn, which is the other structural rule: keep individual golden files small and focused (one report, one scenario), so a regeneration diff is a page, not a phone book. A giant golden file is an invitation to rubber-stamp.

Socially: when a golden test fails, the first hypothesis is "my code regressed," not "the golden file is stale" — because the failures you most care about (a total quietly dropped, a column silently widened) look exactly like staleness. The two incidents you describe are the known failure mode of the technique; the fix is not better tooling but the standing rule that whoever regenerates must be able to explain every changed line, in the commit message, in terms of the intended behavior change. If they can't, the diff is a bug report.

What should the anatomy of a generated report be? Ours is a title and then a wall of numbers, and readers keep asking what period it covers and where the data came from.

Five parts, in order, each answering one reader question. The title says what this is — "Sales Report" — and nothing else; it is a label, not a summary. The context line answers your readers' actual questions: the period covered, the source of the data, and any scope limit, in one or two lines directly under the title ("2026-11-01 to 2026-11-26 · source: orders table · all regions"). A report without a context line cannot be interpreted a week later, and most "the numbers look wrong" escalations are really "I assumed a different period."

The body is the data, grouped the way readers think about it, with each group labeled. Totals follow the body they total — grand totals at the end, subtotals at the end of their groups, never floating in a header where they cannot be checked against the rows. The footer carries notes: definitions that affect reading ("amounts in USD, returns excluded"), exceptions, and the generation facts a auditor wants (generated at, by which version) — kept out of the body's way but never omitted.

Two principles run through it. Order is by reader need: identity, context, evidence, sums, caveats. And every number must be traceable to a computation over the stated source — if a figure in the footer (an average, a count) cannot be pointed at the rows or the query that produced it, it does not belong in the report. The wall of numbers fails not because it is ugly but because it is uninterpretable: nobody can say what it covers, so nobody can say whether it is right.
